A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset-alignment research, despite the revised title. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector evaluations, resizing and compression experiments, shader-based training results, and dataset-size ablations in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds AP/TPR evaluations, architecture and initialization comparisons, and additional corruption-sensitivity experiments.

M1.justification: The reconstruction procedure, binary cross-entropy objective, and Ours/Ours-Sync training remain unchanged. Appendix A.2.4 adds architectural variants for the ablations, including Wide-ResNet, ViT-B/16, and a CLIP ResNet whose attention pooling is replaced with adaptive average pooling.

E1.justification: The training datasets and evaluated image sources, including shaders and FLUX, are retained. Appendix A.2.5 modestly extends input-condition coverage through Gaussian-noise testing and isolated blur/JPEG severity sweeps; Gaussian noise previously appeared as training augmentation, without this evaluation.

E2.justification: The five named external baselines in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. Table 8 adds matched Corvi-dataset comparison variants using alternative architectures and initializations alongside corresponding aligned-data detectors. DRCT is newly discussed in related work but is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2.3 adds AP and per-generator TPR@5% FPR evaluations pooling clean and post-processed images, with 6000 real images and 6000 images per generator. Additional protocols vary architecture and initialization, use 224×224 crops for ViT, and independently sweep corruption severity. Existing experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine whether conclusions depend on decision thresholds, detector architecture or initialization, and individual blur, noise, and JPEG perturbations (A.2.3–A.2.5). These substantially extend the robustness evidence. The dataset-size and computational-efficiency studies are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging two training seeds for the principal natural-image experiments and five for shader experiments. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars, or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: All five original numerical tables retain their values after matching renumbering. New Tables 6–8 and Figures 6–8 substantially expand the results: Table 7 reports Playground TPR@5% FPR of 65.75 for Corvi and 92.88 for Ours-Sync, while the corruption plots reveal strong blur resistance for Ours-Sync but collapsing fake-image scores under increasing noise.

T1.justification: The mathematical setup and reconstruction-based definition of the fake-image distribution are unchanged. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs, and the added evaluation metrics and empirical explanations introduce no new mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The central claims about alignment, inexpensive VAE reconstruction, robustness, and shader-based training remain. The revised introduction explicitly prioritizes reliable detection of fully generated LDM images, excludes partial inpainting, and deemphasizes generalization to unseen generators, modestly narrowing the stated scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving CNN scale dependence, shader threshold calibration, possible CLIP-backbone overfitting, and CNN-versus-ViT behavior. It also interprets the new evaluations as supporting architecture-independent alignment benefits and stronger corruption resistance. The existing WebP and FLUX limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page pointer and implementation information for the new experiments, including initialization sources, pooling changes, ViT crop size, and the blur kernel size. Existing training details remain intact. The reproducibility statement still describes code, dataset, and checkpoint release as intended; actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The related-work section newly identifies DRCT as the closest approach and distinguishes its DDIM reconstruction and dataset alignment from this method. v2 also acknowledges dataset-bias studies by Grommelt and Yan and adds references supporting the architecture ablations. The broader research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, publication header, and contact information and tightens several introductory, related-work, and experimental passages. It promotes the dataset-size study from Appendix A.2.1 to Section 5.4 and moves computational efficiency from Section 5.3 to Appendix A.2.1, while preserving the overall narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds three substantial result tables and three paired corruption-sensitivity figures. It also relocates existing displays, moves the computational-cost figure into the appendix, and enlarges and captions the previously unnumbered WebP plot. The original results remain represented.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–8 strengthen validation beyond the earlier chosen-threshold comparisons and primary ResNet-50 configuration. Separate corruption curves make robustness and failure conditions easier to assess, and the revised scope and DRCT discussion improve positioning. These gains are tempered by broad new robustness interpretations that are not fully supported by the noise failures in Figure 7. Overall, v2 provides useful additional validation without materially changing the established method or principal findings.
